metaDescription: Six battery-powered snow blowers compared from 20 to 24 inches, with pack size, depth, throw and cold-weather runtime explained for real driveways.
expertTake: The EGO SNT2425 two-stage is the most capable battery machine here and the only one that behaves like a small gas unit. The WORX WG461 and Greenworks 80V are the best single-stage values for a normal paved drive. Skip battery machines if your snow is routinely deep, wet and plowed into a berm. Always check how many packs ship in the box. Add a second set of packs if your drive takes more than twenty minutes.
introParagraphs: Battery power has moved from small shovels to full-size machines, and the best ones now rival gas units for typical driveways. They start with a button, make little noise and need no fuel, oil or spark plug. For many owners the biggest change is the morning routine: no priming, no warm-up and no fuel can in the corner of the garage.

The catch is that runtime is limited by what the packs hold, and that power falls in the cold. Choosing well means looking past the headline voltage and comparing pack capacity, path width and whether the design is one stage or two. It also pays to compare what is in the box, because some listings include two packs and a charger while others sell the machine bare.

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2425 24-inch two-stage, 2 x 7.5Ah kit

specList.label: Rated coverage
specList.value: Up to 18 cars in 8 in snow

products.description:
This is the battery machine that behaves most like a gas two-stage. A separate auger and impeller handle breaking and throwing, so it can take a berm and deeper snow than the single-stage models here. The listing claims up to a 50-foot throw and about an 18-car driveway on two packs in 8 inches of snow.

Against the single-stage WORX and Greenworks machines it costs more and weighs more, and it is the only one that can handle a plow ridge without a shovel. Its Peak Power mode combines both packs to boost output, which is why EGO says it matches gas power.

Ownership is simple but not free of care: store the packs indoors, charge them before the forecast and clear jams with the packs removed. If your drive is long or the snow routinely deep, this is the one to buy. Check the weight against your garage floor and any steps before ordering, because a two-stage battery machine is a big machine.
products.bestFor: Long drives and deep snow where a single-stage would struggle.
pros: Two-stage design handles berms and deep snow
No fuel, oil or pull cord
cons: Heavier and more costly than a single-stage
Runtime still limited by the packs in wet snow

products.name: EGO Power+ SNT2122 21-inch single-stage, 2 x 4Ah
products.description:
The SNT2122 is a single-stage machine with variable auger speed and a 180-degree chute, rated for about a 10-car driveway in 8 inches of snow on its two 4Ah packs. It is lighter than the 24-inch two-stage and easier to store.

Variable speed lets you run the auger slowly in light snow to save charge, then open it up for deeper piles. That is a genuine runtime lever on a battery machine. Against the WORX WG461 it has a stronger platform pedigree but a narrower 21-inch path in a different pack system.

It shares packs with EGO mowers and trimmers, so existing owners pay less. Keep it on paved surfaces, since a single-stage auger throws gravel. If your drive is longer than about four cars, plan on a second set of packs or step up to the two-stage.
products.bestFor: Paved drives that want a lighter machine on a shared battery platform.
pros: Lighter and easier to store than a two-stage
cons: 4Ah packs limit runtime on a long drive

products.name: Greenworks 80V 20-inch brushless snow blower, 4Ah kit
products.description:
This 80V 20-inch uses a higher system voltage than most battery machines, which lets the brushless motor reach its power with less current draw. A 4Ah pack and a fast charger are in the kit.

Against the 40V machines it has a stronger motor supply, and against the EGO two-stage it is lighter and simpler. The single pack is the weak point on a long drive, so budget for a second one.

It works best on paved drives and walks with light to moderate snow. Keep the pack indoors until the first pass. Measure the time your usual clear takes first, then decide whether a second pack is part of the budget.
products.bestFor: Paved drives where a higher-voltage motor matters and a second pack is affordable.
cons: Only one pack in the kit

products.name: WORX WG461 40V 20-inch cordless snow blower, 2 x 6Ah
products.description:
The WG461 clears 20 inches wide and 10 inches deep with a brushless single-stage motor and throws up to 35 feet. Two 20V 6Ah PowerShare Pro batteries are in the kit and are rated for large driveways in 6 inches of snow.

Its combination of 6Ah packs and a 35-foot throw makes it the best-balanced single-stage 40V machine here. Against the STEELITE it carries larger packs and a farther throw, and against the Greenworks 80V it has two packs rather than one.

The 20V packs are the standard Worx size and fit many other tools, which stretches their value. It is the sensible choice if you already own PowerShare tools and can borrow packs.
products.bestFor: Paved drives where larger packs and a long throw matter.

products.name: STEELITE 40V 20-inch cordless blower, 2 x 4Ah
products.description:
The STEELITE weighs about 26 pounds and clears 20 inches wide with a brushless motor rated for up to 850 pounds per minute. LED lights and a dual safety mechanism are built in.

It is the lightest of the 20-inch machines, which matters for owners who need to lift it into a car or onto a shelf. The tradeoff is smaller 4Ah packs and a lower build tier than the premium platforms.

For a short drive and a budget-minded buyer it is a sensible pick. Check the box contents carefully, since listings vary on whether a charger and both packs are included.
products.bestFor: Short drives and buyers who need a light machine.

products.name: VOLTASK 48V 20-inch cordless blower, 2 x 4Ah, wheels
products.description:
The VOLTASK uses two 48V 4Ah batteries and a brushless motor that drives the auger at 1,900 RPM. The listing quotes up to 30 minutes of continuous runtime, with wheels and dual LED headlights.

It is a good option for buyers who want a higher-voltage system without paying for a premium platform. The tradeoff is thinner support and fewer compatible tools.

Clear in light layers and keep the packs warm. Ask the seller about warranty and replacement paddles before buying, since support is the main risk with a lesser-known brand.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers wanting a higher-voltage cordless machine.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The EGO SNT2425 is a two-stage with an impeller and can handle berms and deeper snow. The WORX WG461, Greenworks 80V and STEELITE are single-stage and clear up to about 10 inches. If your drive sees more than 10 inches or has a plow ridge, the two-stage is the realistic choice. Many buyers regret a single-stage on a long, buried drive. A practical test is to look at the end of your drive after a plow has passed; if a hard ridge forms there, only a two-stage or a shovel will deal with it. Think of a single-stage as a very good broom and a two-stage as a small plow.

Compare amp-hours and voltage together. The EGO kit has two 7.5Ah 56V packs, the WORX two 6Ah 20V packs, the STEELITE two 4Ah 20V packs and the Greenworks one 4Ah 80V pack. A kit with one pack, like the Greenworks, forces a second purchase on a long drive. Rotate your packs after every use so that both age at the same rate, and keep a spare set charged for long clears.

The EGO two-stage clears 24 inches wide. The 20-inch machines clear 20 inches, and the WORX takes a 10-inch depth. Wider saves passes but is heavier. For a two-car drive, 20 inches is the sweet spot. Count the passes on your own drive to see whether the extra width of the two-stage is worth its weight. Wider paths also take more power per pass, which shortens runtime a little.

Throw ranges from 35 feet on the WORX to 42 on the EGO single-stage and 50 on the two-stage. A longer throw reduces re-clearing in wind. Aim the chute downwind first and finish the upwind side last to keep snow from blowing back onto the cleared lane. Throw distance also depends on how wet the snow is and how fast the auger spins.

Lithium output drops sharply near 0 F. Store the packs indoors, install them just before use and let a cold pack warm before charging. Two charged pairs let one rest while the other works. A cold garage is the worst place to charge, so bring packs inside well before you plug them in.

EGO packs power mowers and trimmers, WORX packs power many 20V tools and Greenworks 80V packs power the 80V line. An existing pack lowers the cost, so check which platform you already own before buying. If you have none of these platforms, the kit with the largest packs usually makes the best starting point. A mixed-platform household usually ends up buying the tool that fits the packs it already has.

specDecoder.meaning: Capacity and pressure. Multiply for watt-hours. This is why comparing only volts misleads.
specDecoder.watchFor: A 4Ah 80V pack stores more energy than a 4Ah 20V pack. Do not assume a bigger Ah number means more runtime across platforms.

specDecoder.meaning: A mode that combines two packs for a boost.
specDecoder.watchFor: Used on the EGO machines. It drains packs faster, so large packs benefit most.

specDecoder.meaning: A separate auger and impeller with wheel drive.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the EGO SNT2425 here. It is the main reason for the higher weight.

specDecoder.meaning: How tall a pile can enter in one pass.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WORX lists 10 inches. Deeper intake helps with settled snow.

specDecoder.meaning: A maker rating of snow capacity. It is a useful comparison between siblings but not a promise.
specDecoder.watchFor: 850 on the STEELITE; treat as relative. Use it for comparing siblings only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Machine design
howWeEvaluated.description: We split the lineup into one two-stage and five single-stage machines. Design decides what snow depth each can handle. This is the single biggest factor for deep snow.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery energy
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared pack capacity and voltage together, from one 4Ah 80V pack to two 7.5Ah 56V packs. A bigger pack also adds weight to carry. We also checked whether each listing includes a charger, because a bare tool needs a separate purchase.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width and throw
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared widths of 20 to 24 inches and throws of 35 to 50 feet. These set the number of passes and how far snow lands. Wind and wet snow shorten throw.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership burden
howWeEvaluated.description: Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, we weighed pack storage and charging. Battery machines avoid fuel but add pack care. A cold battery can look empty before it is.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit to driveway
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each model to a drive length and snow depth. This is an editorial assessment, not a measured score. We recommend buying for your worst storm. Most buyers will be happiest if they pick for the worst storm they expect each winter.

howToChoose.intro: Snow depth is the first filter because a single-stage auger has a hard ceiling that no battery can lift.
Battery kits vary far more in cost than the machines themselves, so compare what each box includes.

cards.label: Single-stage
cards.text: The WORX, Greenworks, STEELITE, VOLTASK and EGO SNT2122 use an auger that scrapes the pavement. They are light and cheap but stop at about 10 inches. Because the auger touches the ground, it also leaves the cleanest surface on pavement.

cards.label: Two-stage
cards.text: The EGO SNT2425 separates auger and impeller. It handles berms and deeper snow but weighs more and costs more. The impeller throws farther and the drive wheels carry the weight, so the operator only steers.

howToChoose.note: Choose single-stage for paved drives with moderate snow; choose two-stage for long drives and deep snow. A common setup is a single-stage for everyday storms and a shovel for berms.

howToChoose.intro: Pack platform matters if you already own cordless tools, because a shared pack can save the cost of a second set.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Large packs and a wide path, or a second set of packs. A long drive can drain a small pack mid-pass. If the drive is steep, also check whether the machine is self-propelled.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EGO SNT2425 has the biggest packs, and the WORX WG461 adds 6Ah packs in a single-stage. The VOLTASK and STEELITE, with smaller packs, are better for shorter runs.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You have a long drive or deep snow. The EGO two-stage is the strongest here. Buying a second pair of packs is cheaper than buying a bigger machine.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a short paved drive. The STEELITE or VOLTASK will do. Light snow and smooth pavement make the smaller packs perfectly adequate.

maintenance.why: Cold reduces output and slows charging. A warm closet is better than a garage. Keep spare packs charged and ready.
A half-charged pack stalls mid-drive. Charge in a warm room so the cells accept the current. A pack that starts warm runs longer.
Rubber tips wear and lose bite. Replace paddles in sets. Check them for cracks as well as wear.
Slush freezes overnight. A quick wipe takes less than a minute.
A stalled auger can restart. Wait for the auger to stop before touching anything.

faq.q: Can a cordless blower replace gas?
faq.a: For paved drives with moderate snow, yes. For deep snow and berms, only the two-stage models come close. Owners who clear for neighbours often keep a gas unit for the worst days. A battery machine also removes the fuel upkeep that makes gas ownership a chore.

faq.q: How long do the packs last?
faq.a: It depends on snow depth and wetness. Makers quote times for light snow, so plan for less in wet snow. Make shallow passes in heavy snow to save charge. A fresh pair gives the longest run, so charge both the night before.

Single-stage is lighter and cheaper but limited to about 10 inches. Two-stage handles more. A common compromise is a single-stage for paved drives. If you are unsure, check what a plow leaves at the end of your drive.

faq.q: Will it work in deep cold?
faq.a: Output drops near 0 F. Keep packs indoors until use. Charging cold packs can damage cells, so warm them first. A pack left in an unheated shed can show a false low charge.

faq.q: Do I need a second set of packs?
faq.a: On a long drive, yes. A spare set lets one charge while the other works. Two charged pairs are the cheapest way to extend runtime.
No. Single-stage augers throw stones. Use a shovel for gravel edges. Clear the paved part with the blower and shovel the stones.
